title: India Invites Pakistan Minister to SCO Forum, First Since Operation Sindoor
excerpt: Aurangzeb Khan Khichi is invited to the November 20-22 Civilisational Dialogue Forum in New Delhi — the first senior Pakistani invitation since the May 2025 confrontation.
body:
• India has invited Pakistan's Minister for National Heritage and Culture, Aurangzeb Khan Khichi, to the first SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum in New Delhi from November 20 to 22.
  • It is the first invitation to a senior Pakistani minister since Operation Sindoor, India's May 2025 military operation after the Pahalgam terror attack.
  • All 10 SCO member states have been invited; Pakistan has not yet confirmed who will attend, or whether Khichi will travel or join by video link.
  • If Khichi travels, it would be the first visit by a senior Pakistani minister to India since Bilawal Bhutto Zardari attended the SCO foreign ministers' meeting in Goa in May 2023.

India has invited a senior Pakistani minister to New Delhi for the first time since the military confrontation of May 2025. Pakistan's Minister for National Heritage and Culture, Aurangzeb Khan Khichi, is among the invitees to the inaugural Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Civilisational Dialogue Forum, to be held in New Delhi from November 20 to 22, according to diplomatic sources cited by The CSR Journal and other Indian outlets. The invitation, issued on October 28, extends to all 10 SCO member states.

What the forum is

The forum, proposed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi at the SCO leaders' summit in Tianjin last year and to be inaugurated by him, is organised jointly by India's ministries of culture and external affairs. It will bring heritage heads and cultural ministers together on historical trade routes, ancient cultural links, Buddhist heritage routes, archaeological preservation and museum exchanges, with representatives from over 25 countries expected at Purana Quila in Delhi. Defence Minister Rajnath Singh announced it at the SCO Council of Heads of Government meeting in Dushanbe, Tajikistan, on October 20.

https://x.com/IndianExpress/status/2115304003374579741

"At the end of this year, India will host the first SCO Civilisation Dialogue Forum. We invite all SCO countries to participate in it."

— Rajnath Singh, Defence Minister, in Dushanbe on October 20

The backdrop: Sindoor and a frozen relationship

Operation Sindoor was launched on May 7, 2025, after the Pahalgam terror attack killed 26 people. Indian forces struck nine terror camps in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, and the confrontation lasted four days before a ceasefire on May 10. Bilateral engagement has been minimal since. At the same Dushanbe meeting where he announced the forum, Singh — with Pakistan's Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar present — called for a unified approach to terrorism.

"There should be no double standards in dealing with terrorism, and no place for those who finance, support or provide safe havens to terrorists. The entire ecosystem of terrorism must be firmly and collectively dismantled."

— Rajnath Singh, Defence Minister

Why the SCO still functions

The SCO has remained a working channel even as bilateral talks have stalled for more than a decade. In October 2024, External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar visited Islamabad for the SCO Council of Heads of Government meeting — the first visit by an Indian foreign minister to Pakistan in nine years. Weeks before this invitation, India sent its SCO national coordinator, Alok Dimri, to Pakistan for a meeting to finalise the grouping's agenda. The pattern is consistent: multilateral obligations are honoured, including hosting duties that require inviting every member, while substantive bilateral discussion stays frozen.

What to watch

Islamabad's response is the open question. Khichi could travel to Delhi, join by video link, send a lower-level delegation, or decline. Each option carries a signal: a ministerial visit would be the most senior Pakistani presence in India in three and a half years, while a video appearance would keep the forum complete without a breakthrough. Either way, the invitation itself — routine as a hosting obligation, significant as the first since Sindoor — marks the current ceiling of India-Pakistan engagement: cultural and multilateral, not bilateral.
